title: Asteroid (14331) Alyankovic: Weird Al Yankovic Gets a Space Rock Named After Him
summary:
Weird Al Yankovic has won five Grammys, had a #1 comedy album, and earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Now he can add something even more out-of-this-world to his resume: an asteroid.

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially approved the name Asteroid (14331) Alyankovic earlier this month. The naming citation was published in the WGSBN Bulletin and the Minor Planet Center. Asteroid names usually honor scientists, but sometimes the scientific community recognizes people outside of science whose work has inspired curiosity and learning.

"The asteroid science community believes Weird Al's influence extends far beyond music," said Dr. Allison McGraw, a planetary scientist at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston. "Many of us grew up listening to Weird Al's music while learning about computers, science, mathematics, and technology. For countless scientists, engineers, programmers, educators, and students, his work helped create an environment where being enthusiastic about learning was something worth celebrating."

The asteroid was discovered by Stephen J. Bus at the Siding Spring Observatory in Australia on March 2, 1981. It is located in the Main Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter and has an estimated diameter of roughly 1 to 1.25 miles. It takes about 1,378 Earth days to orbit the sun. It is a silicate (S-type) asteroid, a type that makes up about 17 percent of all known asteroids.

Weird Al responded with his usual humor: "This is perhaps the greatest honor I've ever received. I just hope this isn't the asteroid that winds up destroying the Earth."

Why does this matter? It shows that science and fun are not opposites. Sometimes a funny song is exactly what makes a kid want to learn about space.
why_it_matters: It is a reminder that science is not only done by serious people in quiet labs — the pop culture a teenager already loves can be the same thing that makes them curious enough to study space, code or physics later on.

background_read: Asteroids are rocky leftovers from the birth of the solar system, and most of them travel around the sun in the Main Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter. Astronomers have found more than a million of them, but only a small share have ever been given names.

The International Astronomical Union (the worldwide group of astronomers that officially names objects in space) usually gives asteroids the names of scientists, but it has also honoured people from outside science — there are asteroids named after each member of the Beatles, for example.
The new name was announced in the WGSBN Bulletin (the newsletter of the IAU's Working Group for Small Bodies Nomenclature, the committee that handles names for asteroids and comets).

Weird Al Yankovic (an American musician famous for funny parody versions of hit songs, played on accordion) fits that pattern: he is known for songs about computers and nerd culture, and Dr. Allison McGraw of the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston says many scientists grew up listening to him.

perspectives.description: Astronomers say the name is deserved because Weird Al's music made curiosity feel normal for a generation of scientists, engineers and programmers. For them an asteroid is a small but official way of saying that humour and learning belong together.

Some researchers argue that names are limited and should go to people who actually studied the sky, and that celebrity naming risks turning a scientific catalogue into a fan contest. They point out that most known asteroids never get a name at all.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the long tradition of cultural naming
perspectives.description: The IAU has always mixed science and culture: asteroids carry the names of astronomers, but also of artists, writers, mythological figures and even the Beatles. Naming is partly about deciding whose work a community wants to remember decades later.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what the name might do
perspectives.description: The real test comes later: whether a silly song actually pushes a student toward a physics class, or whether the honour becomes a one-day news story. Either way, the rock will keep that name as long as anyone is watching it.
